bib.title: Data Wrangling: Join, Combine, and Reshape (Chapter 8)
bib.first_author: unknown (not printed in the chapter text)
bib.venue: book chapter (page numbers 221-251; book title not printed in the extracted text)

question: How do you combine, join and rearrange tabular data in pandas using hierarchical indexing, merge, join, concat, combine_first, stack/unstack, pivot and melt?
contributions: Hierarchical indexing (MultiIndex) with partial indexing, swaplevel, sort_index, level-wise statistics, set_index/reset_index
Database-style joins with pandas.merge, DataFrame.join, concat and combine_first
Reshaping with stack/unstack, pivot (long to wide) and melt (wide to long)

results.claim: A many-to-many merge forms the Cartesian product of the matching key rows.
results.setup: pd.merge(df1, df2, on='key', how='left'); df1 has 3 'b' rows, df2 has 2 (In [45]-[49])
results.quote:
Many-to-many joins form the Cartesian product of the rows. Since there were three
'b' rows in the left DataFrame and two in the right one, there are six 'b' rows in the
result.

results.claim: merge defaults to an inner join (intersection of keys); 'c' and 'd' rows drop out.
results.setup: In [39]-[43], df1/df2 with keys b,a,c vs a,b,d
results.quote:
By default merge does an 'inner' join; the keys in the result are the intersec‐
tion, or the common set found in both tables.

results.claim: Without on=, merge uses overlapping column names as keys; the author advises specifying it explicitly.
results.quote:
It’s a good practice to
specify explicitly, though:

results.claim: DataFrame.join performs a left join on the keys, preserving the left row index, unlike merge's default inner join.
results.quote:
DataFrame’s join
method performs a left join on the join keys, exactly preserving the left frame’s row
index.

results.claim: When joining columns-on-columns, indexes of the passed DataFrames are discarded.
results.quote:
When you’re joining columns-on-columns, the indexes on the
passed DataFrame objects are discarded.

results.claim: Selection on a hierarchically indexed object is much faster if the index is lexicographically sorted from the outermost level.
results.quote:
Data selection performance is much better on hierarchically
indexed objects if the index is lexicographically sorted

results.claim: stack drops missing data by default so that stack inverts unstack; dropna=False keeps it.

results.quote:
Note that pivot is equivalent to creating a hierarchical index using set_index fol‐

results.claim: melt is the inverse of pivot: it merges several columns into one, giving a longer frame; id_vars marks group indicators and value_vars selects value columns.
results.quote: An inverse operation to pivot for DataFrames is pandas.melt.

limits: Code is from an older pandas: uses MultiIndex labels=, sum(level=), join_axes=, pivot positional args and b[-1]=...; several are removed or deprecated in current pandas.
Table 8-1 prints 'output' where the text and code use 'outer'.
In [132] repeats data2.unstack() where the preceding sentence describes stack's default.
righth in In [65] lists Ohio 2000 twice with different rows (printed output shows duplicate index values, which is what the next example demonstrates).
Examples are toy data with no timing or scale; only the sort_index performance remark touches speed, with no number.
practices: Specify the join key explicitly with on= rather than relying on overlapping column names (p.228).
Use how='outer' to keep the union of keys; default is 'inner' (p.229, Table 8-2).
Use suffixes=('_left','_right') to disambiguate overlapping non-key column names in merge (p.231).
Pass a list of column names to merge on multiple keys; think of them as an array of tuples (p.230-231).
Use left_on/right_on when key names differ and left_index/right_index when a key is in the index (p.228, 232).
With hierarchically indexed right frames, pass multiple left_on columns plus right_index=True (p.234).
Use join on indexes, or pass a list of frames to join, for simple index-on-index merges (p.235-236).
Use concat with keys= to keep the pieces identifiable, names= to name the levels, and ignore_index=True when the row index carries no data (p.238-240).
Use join='inner' in concat to intersect the other axes (p.237-238).
Use combine_first to patch missing values in one object with values from another (p.241-242).
Sort a MultiIndex lexicographically from the outermost level (sort_index(level=0)) before selecting (p.225).
Use pivot to go long to wide and melt for wide to long; reset_index after pivot to move the row labels back into a column (p.247-250).
